narrativeReportMd:
# CarePlan R4→R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
CarePlan has material local breaking changes. The highest-impact changes are the removal of inline `activity.detail`, the reshaping/renaming of activity references and outcomes, the same-name datatype replacement for `addresses`, and the `author`→`custodian` rename. R6 also widens important workflow terminology and reference targets, creating R6→R4 representability and runtime enum/dispatch risks.

## Scope
This assessment covers the base CarePlan resource in the local R4 and R6 core packages. Inherited Resource/DomainResource/Element/Extension changes are called out as out of scope and not counted as CarePlan findings.

## Main migration themes
1. CarePlan no longer carries some request-like information inline. R4 `activity.detail` data usually needs promotion to a real request resource referenced from `activity.plannedActivityReference`.
2. Several properties are not wire-compatible even when the clinical idea survives: `activity.reference` becomes `plannedActivityReference`, outcomes become `performedActivity`, `author` becomes `custodian`, and `addresses` becomes `CodeableReference`.
3. R6 can express workflow states and links that R4 cannot represent directly, including `status=ended`, `intent=directive`, broader `basedOn` targets, concept-only `addresses`, and RequestOrchestration references.

## Highest-impact findings
The most disruptive R4→R6 validation breaks are `CarePlan.activity.detail` removal, `CarePlan.addresses` datatype replacement, `CarePlan.activity.reference` rename, and outcome-to-performedActivity replacement. These affect serialized instances, generated classes, validators, FHIRPath expressions, and business rules.

## Findings requiring human review
Human review is most important for mapping inline activity details, interpreting outcomes versus performed activities, preserving root instantiates links, and converting R6-only lifecycle/intent values back to R4.

## Backward-compatible design observations
Several changes could have been staged with deprecated aliases or added sibling elements. The R6 model is generally cleaner and more expressive, but it prioritizes model cleanup over wire compatibility for common CarePlan surfaces.

## Follow-up analysis
Review base Resource/DomainResource reports for inherited changes, CodeableReference for cross-artifact serialization impacts, RequestGroup→RequestOrchestration migration, and official terminology/ConceptMap guidance when available.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: CarePlan has high-impact local breaking changes, especially around activity modeling and `addresses` serialization. Top migration concerns are converting inline `activity.detail` to referenced request resources, renaming/reshaping activity and responsibility fields, and handling R6-only workflow codes/targets. The main uncertainty is the intended official replacement for removed root instantiates links and exact semantic guidance for outcome-to-performedActivity migration.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Migration is less about cardinality tightening and more about representation changes. R4 systems that embedded plan activity details must create or reference separate request resources. R4 `Reference`/`CodeableConcept` pairs are consolidated into R6 `CodeableReference` in key places, changing JSON shape and generated types. R6 widens workflow semantics, so reverse conversion to R4 needs explicit policy for `ended`, `directive`, broader `basedOn` targets, concept-only addresses, and RequestOrchestration.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for structural findings because both local StructureDefinitions were present and directly compared. Confidence is medium for some semantic and justification judgments because no official R4→R6 diff, narrative migration page, or ConceptMap was available locally. Terminology comparison used packaged ValueSet compose and CodeSystem concepts, not live terminology expansions.

findings.title: CarePlan.addresses changed from Reference(Condition) to CodeableReference with broader targets

semanticText.definition: Identifies the conditions/problems/concerns/diagnoses/etc. whose management and/or mitigation are handled by this plan.

oldState.narrativeMd: In R4 each `CarePlan.addresses` repetition serializes directly as a `Reference`, normally such as `{ "reference": "Condition/123" }`.

newState.summary: 0..* CodeableReference to a concept or to Condition, Procedure, or MedicationAdministration.

binding.description: Codes that describe the health issues this plan addresses.

semanticText.comment: Use CarePlan.addresses.concept when a code sufficiently describes the concern; use CarePlan.addresses.reference when referencing a resource.

newState.narrativeMd: In R6 each repetition is a `CodeableReference`, so a resource reference is nested under `addresses.reference`, and a terminology-only concern may be carried in `addresses.concept`.

facts.note: The element name is unchanged but the value type is not wire-compatible.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element id and path are unchanged, but its datatype changed from `Reference` to `CodeableReference`.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a direct wire-format break for R4 instances that populate `addresses`: the JSON object that was a `Reference` in R4 is not a valid `CodeableReference` in R6 unless wrapped under `reference`. R6 also permits concept-only concerns and additional target resource types that cannot be represented by the R4 base element without extensions or lossy conversion.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Losing or mis-shaping the concern addressed by a plan can affect clinical decision support, care coordination, and plan filtering.

justification.inferredGoal: Allow CarePlan to address coded concerns and event/procedure/administration resources, not only Condition resources.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain R4 `addresses` as Reference(Condition) and add a new optional CodeableReference concern element, or stage the replacement through a deprecated alias.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Allowing CarePlan to address coded concerns and broader concern resources is a reasonable R6 goal, and `CodeableReference` is the R6 idiom for concept-or-reference content. The same-path type replacement is still a real wire-format break for populated R4 `addresses`. A less-breaking base design exists, but it would leave two ways to represent the same concern and would have material long-term interoperability costs, so the breaking design is probably justified rather than clearly avoidable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The strongest less-breaking base design would keep `CarePlan.addresses` as `Reference(Condition)` for R4 compatibility and add an optional `CodeableReference` sibling for coded concerns plus Procedure and MedicationAdministration references. That would preserve old instances, but the old and new same-resource fields would overlap. Implementers could populate either or both, the deprecated representation might never disappear, and search, profiling, and validation rules would need to reconcile both shapes.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: This would preserve R4 references but create overlapping concern representations and ambiguity for search, validation, and migration.

evidence.detail: R4 type is Reference with targetProfile Condition.
R6 type is CodeableReference with targetProfiles Condition, Procedure, and MedicationAdministration.
CodeableReference contains separate concept and reference children, changing JSON shape from a bare Reference.

examples.examplesMd: Examples are focused fragments with required CarePlan fields included; the key compatibility point is the shape of `addresses`.

findings.narrativeMd: `CarePlan.addresses` retained its path but changed datatype. That is easy for humans to miss because the element name is stable, but generated models, serializers, validators, and FHIRPath expressions that expect a `Reference` now need a `CodeableReference`. Existing R4 JSON with `addresses[].reference` at the top level of each repetition becomes invalid in R6; R6 content can also use a coded concern without a referenced resource.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4→R6: an R4-valid `addresses` reference is old-valid/new-invalid unless transformed to `addresses.reference`. R6→R4: concept-only concerns and references to Procedure or MedicationAdministration are not valid in the R4 base element. Codegen risk is high because the property type changed while the element name stayed the same.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Transform each R4 `addresses` item to `CodeableReference.reference`. For R6→R4, map Condition references directly, but use an extension, supporting resource, or manual review for concept-only concerns and non-Condition references. Tests should include Condition references, concept-only addresses, and the new Procedure/MedicationAdministration target cases.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The broader model is useful, but a same-name type replacement is one of the more disruptive approaches. A sibling optional element or a transition period retaining a Reference-shaped field would have been more wire-compatible, at the cost of duplicate representations.

freshReview.narrativeMd: The unchanged element path hides a real wire-format break: an R4 `addresses` item is a direct `Reference`, while R6 expects a `CodeableReference` with either a nested `reference` or a `concept`. Generated models, FHIRPath, and serializers must change, and R6 can now express concept-only concerns or non-Condition references that R4 cannot. Still, the R6 goal is coherent: a care plan concern may be a coded problem or a referenced clinical resource, and `CodeableReference` is the base R6 pattern for that. Keeping both the old Reference field and a new concept/reference concern field would preserve old instances but create duplicate concern representations.
keyEvidence: R4 CarePlan.addresses is 0..* Reference constrained to Condition.
R6 CarePlan.addresses is 0..* CodeableReference targeting Condition, Procedure, or MedicationAdministration.
R6 CarePlan.addresses adds an example binding to clinical-findings and comments distinguishing addresses.concept from addresses.reference.
freshReview.fmmEffect: R4 CarePlan is FMM 2 and trial-use, so maturity is neutral under the framework. The hard break matters, but FMM 2 does not by itself make a coherent CodeableReference modernization suspect.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: R4 JSON with addresses[n].reference as a direct Reference is not the R6 CodeableReference shape; R6 concept-only and non-Condition references also create R6-to-R4 loss.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Partial. R6 could have retained Reference(Condition) at `addresses` and added a new optional CodeableReference concern element, or kept the old form as a deprecated alias. That would preserve many R4 instances, but it would split one clinical concern across overlapping fields and complicate search, profiling, and duplicate/conflict handling.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing High impact and Partial alternative judgment; the fresh review agrees the break is real but treats the R6 design as proportionate rather than needing renewed standards attention.

findings.title: Inline CarePlan.activity.detail backbone was removed

oldState.summary: Optional inline BackboneElement for planned activity details with many child fields; `detail.status` was mandatory when detail was present.

constraints.human: Provide a reference or detail, not both

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 allowed a CarePlan activity to be described inline using `activity.detail`, including kind, code, status, scheduled[x], location, performer, product[x], quantity, dailyAmount, description, doNotPerform, goals, and reasons.

newState.summary: No `activity.detail` element exists in R6; planned activity details are expected to be represented by another request resource referenced from `plannedActivityReference`.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 removed the inline detail backbone from CarePlan. The surviving planned-activity mechanism is a reference to a dedicated resource, plus separate performed-activity tracking.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: No R6 element preserves the inline detail backbone. Several R4 child fields have conceptual homes in specific request resources, but not as children of CarePlan.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Any R4 instance containing `activity.detail` uses an element that is absent in R6, so strict R6 validation fails. The migration is not merely a rename: inline detail fields must usually be promoted into a referenced request resource, and some details may require different target resources or extensions.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: CarePlan activity details can include intended interventions, timing, performers, products, quantities, reasons, and negation (`doNotPerform`); losing or mis-mapping them can change care instructions.

justification.inferredGoal: Reduce duplicated request-like content inside CarePlan and require planned activities to use the appropriate request resource.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain deprecated `activity.detail` in base R6 while recommending referenced request resources for new planned activities.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred goal of removing partial request-like content from CarePlan is reasonable because inline `activity.detail` duplicates concepts that belong on request resources with their own identity and lifecycle. Keeping the backbone would be much less breaking, but it would materially undercut that cleanup by preserving a parallel same-resource representation for planned activity details. Given that tradeoff, the removal is probably justified, though it remains a high-impact migration break.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design would keep `CarePlan.activity.detail` as optional and deprecated, retain the mutual-exclusion rule with the reference element, and document that new R6 content should use `plannedActivityReference` to an appropriate request resource. This would let old instances validate, but it would prolong the ambiguous embedded-request pattern and force consumers to support both inline and referenced activity models indefinitely.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: This preserves embedded R4 activities but continues duplicate request-like modeling and unclear lifecycle ownership inside CarePlan.

evidence.detail: R4 defines `activity.detail` as a 0..1 BackboneElement.
R4 detail includes fields such as status, scheduled[x], doNotPerform, performer, product[x], quantity, and description.
No matching R6 element id exists.

examples.examplesMd: The migration example is intentionally partial: a real migration must create or identify the referenced request resource and place timing, status, performer, product, and negation details in fields appropriate to that resource.

findings.narrativeMd: The largest local CarePlan break is the removal of the inline activity detail backbone. R4 systems could put a compact request-like activity directly inside CarePlan; R6 expects the planned activity to live in a referenced request resource. This affects both validation and application architecture because data that used to be embedded may now need separate resource identities and lifecycle management.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4→R6 validation fails whenever `activity.detail` is present. Code generators also lose the nested `CarePlan.activity.detail` class and all of its children. R6→R4 is less direct for this specific removed element, but any R6 data represented through the new referenced-resource pattern will not round-trip into the old inline detail without constructing a synthetic detail and potentially losing resource-specific fields.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Inventory all uses of `activity.detail`. For each activity, choose a target request resource such as ServiceRequest, MedicationRequest, NutritionOrder, DeviceRequest, CommunicationRequest, Task, Appointment, or VisionPrescription, then map R4 child fields to that resource. Pay special attention to `doNotPerform`, `scheduled[x]`, status/statusReason, performer, product, quantity/dailyAmount, goals, and reasons. Where no target field exists, use an extension or retain the original R4 data for manual review.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The removal probably reflects a deliberate move away from partial inline request representations. It is nevertheless avoidable as a hard break: the old backbone could have remained deprecated while R6 encouraged references. That alternative would have preserved old instances but would continue allowing divergent representations of the same planned activity.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Migration quality depends heavily on the chosen target request resource and is not determinable from CarePlan alone.

freshReview.narrativeMd: Removing `activity.detail` is more than a property rename. R4 allowed a complete inline planned-activity summary with status, timing, negation, performer, product, quantity, reasons, goals, and description. R6 has no inline replacement, so migration often requires creating or selecting a separate request resource and moving each child into resource-specific fields. That can be expert-dependent and safety-relevant, especially for `doNotPerform`, timing, product, and quantity. The R6 cleanup goal is understandable, but a transitional base design retaining deprecated inline detail with mutual exclusion against `plannedActivityReference` looks plausible enough to warrant renewed review.
keyEvidence: R4 CarePlan.activity.detail is 0..1 BackboneElement.

R4 detail has children including kind, code, reasonCode, reasonReference, goal, status, statusReason, doNotPerform, scheduled[x], location, performer, product[x], dailyAmount, quantity, and description.
R6 CarePlan has activity.plannedActivityReference and performedActivity, but no CarePlan.activity.detail element.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral: it does not impose normative stability, but it also does not soften this to an experimental-change concern. The path-level migration burden and clinical meaning dominate.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: any R4 instance with activity.detail contains an element absent from R6; generated nested detail classes and validators also break.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Yes, with tradeoffs. R6 could keep `activity.detail` as optional and deprecated, preserving the existing mutual-exclusion pattern with the planned activity reference. That would prolong the embedded-request model and require consumers to support two activity representations, but it would preserve old instances and reduce lossy or expert-dependent migration.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing High impact and Partial alternative judgment, but disagree with treating the removal as probably justified; the fresh review judges the expert-dependent migration and plausible transitional design as Revisit.

findings.title: CarePlan.activity.reference was renamed to plannedActivityReference and its orchestration target changed

oldState.summary: 0..1 Reference to a request-like resource, including RequestGroup.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 used `activity.reference` for details of the proposed activity represented in a specific resource.

newState.summary: 0..1 Reference to the planned activity resource, with RequestOrchestration replacing RequestGroup in the target list.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 uses `activity.plannedActivityReference` for the same planned-activity role. The element definition is close to the old one, but the property name and one target resource changed.

facts.note: The old mutual-exclusion rule with inline detail disappeared because detail was removed.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The R6 element has the same cardinality, same role, nearly the same definition/comment, and the same target list except for the RequestGroup to RequestOrchestration shift.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 instances using `activity.reference` fail R6 validation because the element name no longer exists. The simple case is mechanically renamable, but references to R4 RequestGroup require a separate resource migration to R6 RequestOrchestration. R6 instances with `plannedActivityReference` are likewise not R4-valid without renaming and possible target conversion.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Mis-mapping planned activities can disconnect a care plan from orders or tasks that drive care coordination.

justification.inferredGoal: Clarify that the reference points to a planned activity and align with the R6 RequestOrchestration resource name.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep the R4 `activity.reference` element name, clarify its planned-activity meaning, and update R6 target guidance.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Clarifying that the reference is the planned activity and aligning orchestration targets with R6 are reasonable goals. The hard element rename was not necessary to accomplish those goals: R6 could have lived with the nonoptimal `reference` name while improving its short, definition, comments, and target list. Because that alternative preserves most R4 instances with modest long-term cost, the path rename appears probably avoidable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A backward-compatible base design would leave `CarePlan.activity.reference` in place and update its definition to the R6 planned-activity wording. The target list could be adjusted for R6 resources, with RequestGroup references handled by the separate RequestGroup-to-RequestOrchestration migration. This avoids duplicate same-resource fields and preserves the common non-RequestGroup cases; the main cost is that the element name remains less descriptive than `plannedActivityReference`.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: This would preserve most wire compatibility with the low tradeoff of retaining a generic element name; RequestGroup-to-RequestOrchestration still needs resource migration.

evidence.detail: R4 defines `activity.reference` as a 0..1 Reference to planned activity resources including RequestGroup.
R6 defines `activity.plannedActivityReference` with the same planned-activity role and RequestOrchestration in the target list.
R6 package contains RequestOrchestration; R6 package search found no StructureDefinition-RequestGroup.json.

examples.examplesMd: For non-RequestGroup targets, migration can often rename the property. RequestGroup/RequestOrchestration requires a separate resource-level transform.

findings.narrativeMd: This is a high-confidence rename/replacement. The old R4 element is gone, so existing JSON, XML, FHIRPath, search extraction code, and generated models that refer to `CarePlan.activity.reference` break even though most referenced resource types are still allowed. The target change from RequestGroup to RequestOrchestration adds a second compatibility issue for orchestration-style planned activities.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4→R6: `activity.reference` is an unknown/invalid element in R6. R6→R4: `activity.plannedActivityReference` is unknown in R4, and RequestOrchestration references are outside R4 CarePlan.activity.reference targets. Strict enum/union target handling and FHIRPath expressions must be updated.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Rename `activity.reference` to `activity.plannedActivityReference`. Verify all target resource types, and route RequestGroup references through a RequestGroup→RequestOrchestration migration or preserve them via extension when no lossless mapping is available. Tests should cover every target type in the R4 list.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The clearer name is useful but not strictly necessary for compatibility. Retaining the old name as deprecated would have avoided hard instance breaks while allowing R6 systems to prefer the new name.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `activity.reference` and `activity.plannedActivityReference` have the same cardinality and nearly the same role for non-orchestration targets. For most existing references, the migration is just a wire-name change, which means R4 instances, FHIRPath expressions, generated accessors, and indexes break mainly for terminology cleanup. The RequestGroup to RequestOrchestration target change is a separate resource migration issue, but it did not require renaming the CarePlan property. Retaining `activity.reference` and clarifying its definition would have been a low-cost base-compatible design.
keyEvidence: R4 CarePlan.activity.reference is 0..1 Reference to Appointment, CommunicationRequest, DeviceRequest, MedicationRequest, NutritionOrder, Task, ServiceRequest, VisionPrescription, or RequestGroup.
R6 CarePlan.activity.plannedActivityReference is 0..1 Reference to the same list except RequestOrchestration replaces RequestGroup.
R6 CarePlan has no activity.reference element.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral, so the avoidability of the same-type same-cardinality rename carries the judgment rather than maturity pressure.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: R4 activity.reference is unknown in R6 until renamed; RequestGroup references also need resource-level migration to RequestOrchestration.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Yes. R6 could keep `activity.reference` as the base wire name, update the short/definition to emphasize planned activity, and adjust target guidance for RequestOrchestration. The main cost is retaining a less descriptive property name, which is modest compared with breaking all existing references to the path.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree with the existing High impact and Yes alternative judgment; this remains an avoidable hard path rename.

findings.title: Activity outcome elements were replaced by performedActivity CodeableReference

oldState.summary: Two 0..* elements: outcomeCodeableConcept for coded results and outcomeReference for referenced event/result resources.

binding.description: Identifies the results of the activity.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 separated coded activity outcomes from referenced outcome resources using two sibling elements.

newState.summary: One 0..* CodeableReference element named performedActivity, allowing either concept or Resource reference.

binding.description: Identifies the results of the activity.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 represents completed or in-progress activities as `performedActivity`, with the concept/reference choice inside CodeableReference.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The R6 element mapping text explicitly describes an event outcome of `plannedActivityReference`, and its type combines the old coded/reference alternatives.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 instances using either outcome element are invalid in R6 until converted to `performedActivity.concept` or `performedActivity.reference`. The semantic label also shifted from outcome/result to performed activity, so some outcome codes may not be a clean activity representation even though the binding is only example strength.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Incorrectly converting outcomes into performed activities can change what actually happened versus what resulted from an activity.

justification.inferredGoal: Unify coded and referenced performed activities under CodeableReference and clarify the distinction between planned and performed activity.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep the old outcome elements as deprecated aliases while introducing `performedActivity`, or defer the CodeableReference unification.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Unifying coded and referenced performed activities under `CodeableReference` is a reasonable R6 modeling goal, and the new name better describes activities that actually occurred. A less-breaking design could retain the old outcome elements, but that would perpetuate parallel representations and blur the already-sensitive distinction between an outcome and an activity performed. Those tradeoffs are material enough that the breaking design is probably justified.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best less-breaking base design would allow `outcomeCodeableConcept` and `outcomeReference` as deprecated aliases while adding `performedActivity`, with an invariant or guidance to avoid duplicate entries. That would keep R4 instances valid, but systems would need to reconcile old outcome fields with the new performed-activity field, and deprecated representations could accumulate indefinitely.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: This would preserve R4 outcomes but leave overlapping outcome/performed-activity representations and semantic ambiguity.

evidence.detail: R4 outcomeCodeableConcept is 0..* CodeableConcept bound by example to care-plan-activity-outcome.
R4 outcomeReference is 0..* Reference(Resource).
R6 performedActivity is 0..* CodeableReference(Resource) bound by example to care-plan-activity-performed.
R6 performedActivity example value set is an enumerated SNOMED list; R4 outcome value set used a SNOMED is-a filter.

examples.examplesMd: The mechanical mapping is straightforward, but reviewers should decide whether coded outcomes are truly performed activities or should be represented elsewhere.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 collapses the two R4 outcome elements into a single `performedActivity` CodeableReference. This is structurally breaking because both old element names disappear, and semantically notable because “outcome” and “performed activity” are not always interchangeable. A Procedure reference is likely a clean migration; a text or code saying “patient understands” may be an outcome rather than an activity.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4→R6 validation fails for `outcomeCodeableConcept` and `outcomeReference`. R6→R4 requires splitting CodeableReference values back into either outcomeCodeableConcept or outcomeReference, which is structurally possible for concept/reference values but semantically uncertain for the new performed-activity framing.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Map `outcomeReference` to `performedActivity.reference` and `outcomeCodeableConcept` to `performedActivity.concept`, then review coded outcomes that describe results rather than activities. If the outcome is actually a goal result or observation, consider representing it in the appropriate event or observation resource instead of blindly converting.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A unified CodeableReference is a reasonable R6 design, but removing both old names is avoidable. Keeping deprecated aliases could have allowed old instances to validate while warning implementers to migrate to the new representation.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 split activity outcomes into coded and referenced fields; R6 unifies them as `performedActivity` CodeableReference. That invalidates old element names and changes generated APIs. The semantic label also shifts from outcome/result to activity performed, so coded results should not be mapped blindly. However, the R6 structure matches a real modeling improvement: concept-or-reference values move into one repeating element and the activity performed is separated from goal outcomes. Keeping old outcome fields alongside `performedActivity` would preserve instances but leave overlapping and potentially conflicting activity/result channels.
keyEvidence: R4 CarePlan.activity.outcomeCodeableConcept is 0..* CodeableConcept with an example care-plan-activity-outcome binding.
R4 CarePlan.activity.outcomeReference is 0..* Reference(Resource).
R6 CarePlan.activity.performedActivity is 0..* CodeableReference(Resource) with an example care-plan-activity-performed binding.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral. The optional path still has real migration work, but the maturity level does not require preserving the old split when the replacement has a substantive model rationale.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: R4 outcomeCodeableConcept and outcomeReference are absent in R6; R6 performedActivity values must be split or reviewed for R4 down-conversion.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Partial. Deprecated aliases for outcomeCodeableConcept and outcomeReference could preserve old instances, but they would require merge, ordering, duplicate, and semantic-precedence rules with performedActivity, especially where a coded outcome is not actually an activity.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree with the existing High impact and Partial alternative judgment; the fresh review also agrees the break is proportionate despite needing careful migration for coded outcomes.

findings.title: CarePlan.author was replaced by CarePlan.custodian

oldState.summary: 0..1 Reference to the designated responsible party, named author.

semanticText.definition: When populated, the author is responsible for the care plan. The care plan is attributed to the author.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 used `author` for the party responsible for and attributed with the care plan.

newState.summary: 0..1 Reference to the designated responsible party, named custodian, with the same target profiles.

semanticText.definition: When populated, the custodian is responsible for the care plan. The care plan is attributed to the custodian.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 uses `custodian` for a very similar role, while `author` is absent.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The cardinality, target profiles, summary flag, workflow mapping, and definition are essentially the same, with the responsible party renamed from author to custodian.

impact.impactRationaleMd: A populated R4 `author` element is not valid in R6. The migration is usually a property rename, but the term `custodian` can carry stewardship semantics that are not identical to authorship in local business rules.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Attribution and responsibility fields can drive ownership, workflow routing, and accountability.

justification.inferredGoal: Clarify that the responsible party is custodian/steward rather than literal author.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep `author` and clarify that it denotes the responsible custodian, or add `custodian` while retaining deprecated `author`.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 goal of using custodian/steward terminology is understandable, but the computable definitions show an almost one-to-one replacement with the same cardinality and target profiles. Living with the R4 name plus clearer definition would meet the core responsibility-attribution goal with little interoperability cost. The hard rename therefore appears probably avoidable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A backward-compatible base design would keep `CarePlan.author` and update its short, definition, and comments to state the custodian/responsible-party meaning. If R6 also wanted the `custodian` name, it could add that element with deprecation guidance for `author`, but that introduces temporary duplicate responsibility fields. The simpler low-break alternative is to retain `author` as the wire name and clarify the semantics.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: The less-breaking path has low to moderate cost: the old term persists or responsibility is duplicated during a transition.

evidence.detail: R4 defines author as 0..1 Reference to Patient, Practitioner, PractitionerRole, Device, RelatedPerson, Organization, or CareTeam.
R6 defines custodian with the same cardinality and target profiles.
No R6 author element exists.

examples.examplesMd: The example shows the usual property rename. Local policy should confirm that the R4 author really is the R6 custodian.

findings.narrativeMd: This is a straightforward but breaking element rename. It will affect serialized instances, generated model properties, search/extraction logic, mappings, and UI labels that treat `author` as the responsible party. Most data can be moved to `custodian`, but sites that distinguish the person who authored the content from the organization stewarding it should review the semantics.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4→R6: any instance with `author` is invalid unless the element is renamed to `custodian`. R6→R4: `custodian` is not an R4 CarePlan element but can usually map to `author` with possible semantic narrowing.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Map `CarePlan.author` to `CarePlan.custodian` for base compatibility. Review downstream workflow and audit rules that used “author” to mean creator rather than responsible custodian, and consider preserving creator information in Provenance or extensions if needed.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Because the replacement is so close structurally, retaining `author` as deprecated would have been a low-cost compatibility path. The main tradeoff would be ambiguity between author and custodian until one is retired.

freshReview.narrativeMd: This is a near one-for-one wire rename from `author` to `custodian`: same cardinality, same reference target set, same summary behavior, and very similar responsible-party definition. That makes old instances and generated code fail for what appears mostly to be terminology cleanup. If R6 wanted to clarify stewardship rather than literal authorship, the base model could have kept the `author` wire name and updated its prose, avoiding duplicate fields and preserving R4 data.
keyEvidence: R4 CarePlan.author is 0..1 Reference to Patient, Practitioner, PractitionerRole, Device, RelatedPerson, Organization, or CareTeam.
R6 CarePlan.custodian has the same cardinality and target profiles.
R6 CarePlan has no author element.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral. It does not forbid renames, but it leaves little reason to accept a same-shape rename when a low-cost compatible wording change was available.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: populated R4 author is not a valid R6 CarePlan element; runtime/API/codegen also changes from author to custodian.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Yes. Keep `author` as the wire path and clarify that it means the responsible custodian, or add `custodian` only with a deprecated alias period. The alias version has duplicate-responsibility risk, but simply retaining `author` has low modeling cost.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree with the existing Medium impact and Yes alternative judgment; the fresh review classifies the avoidable rename as Revisit.

findings.title: CarePlan.instantiatesCanonical and instantiatesUri were removed

oldState.summary: Root-level optional canonical and uri links to FHIR-defined or external protocols/definitions adhered to by the CarePlan.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 could state directly on CarePlan that the plan instantiates a protocol, guideline, questionnaire, measure, activity definition, operation definition, or external URI.

newState.summary: No root CarePlan instantiatesCanonical or instantiatesUri element exists in R6.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 CarePlan has no direct replacement element at the root for protocol/definition instantiation.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: Both R4 element ids are absent from the R6 CarePlan StructureDefinition, and no same-level replacement is defined.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 instances that identify protocols or definitions at the CarePlan root become invalid in R6. Unlike a simple rename, the supplied R6 CarePlan definition does not expose an equivalent root element, so preserving the information may require an extension, Provenance, PlanDefinition linkage outside CarePlan, or a referenced request/orchestration resource.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Protocol/definition links can be important for guideline adherence, quality reporting, and explainability.

justification.inferredGoal: Possibly move protocol/definition instantiation to request/orchestration resources or remove workflow-pattern duplication from CarePlan.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain `instantiatesCanonical` and `instantiatesUri` as deprecated root elements while documenting any preferred R6 workflow location.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The local definitions show removal of direct protocol/definition links but do not show an R6 replacement or rationale. Removing the fields is a hard R4-to-R6 break for data that records guideline or definition provenance. A less-breaking base design is plausible, but if the true goal was to move all such links off CarePlan, retaining them would only partially satisfy that goal. On the available evidence, the level of breakage is not clearly justified.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design would keep the optional root `instantiatesCanonical` and `instantiatesUri` elements, mark them deprecated if necessary, and add comments pointing to the preferred R6 representation when a referenced request, RequestOrchestration, PlanDefinition, or Provenance resource is more appropriate. This is a base-design alternative, not merely conversion tooling. Its cost is that legacy root links could remain in use and consumers might need to inspect multiple places for the same protocol relationship.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: This preserves protocol links but weakens any goal to remove workflow-pattern duplication and may leave definition links split across CarePlan and request/orchestration resources.

evidence.detail: R4 defines instantiatesCanonical as 0..* canonical with target profiles including PlanDefinition and ActivityDefinition.
R4 defines instantiatesUri as 0..* uri for externally maintained protocols or guidelines.
Neither element exists in R6 CarePlan.

examples.examplesMd: No lossless base R6 CarePlan transform is shown because the R6 StructureDefinition does not define a replacement root element.

findings.narrativeMd: R4 CarePlan could directly declare which definition or external protocol it followed. R6 removes those root elements. This breaks any instance or generated class using them and creates a semantic migration problem because the information is not just syntactic; it may explain why the plan exists or how conformance to a guideline should be assessed.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4→R6 instances with either instantiates element are invalid. R6 does not create a corresponding new CarePlan element, so this is primarily a loss-of-representation risk rather than an R6→R4 issue.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Do not drop these values silently. Determine whether they belong on a referenced PlanDefinition, RequestOrchestration, ServiceRequest, Provenance, or a standard/custom extension. Validate migrated examples with consumers that rely on guideline/protocol attribution.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The removal may be part of a broader workflow cleanup, but without rationale it appears potentially avoidable. Retaining deprecated fields or defining a cross-version extension would have allowed old data to remain valid while systems migrated to the preferred R6 pattern.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: This finding needs official narrative/change-note confirmation to identify the preferred R6 representation.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 root-level `instantiatesCanonical` and `instantiatesUri` carried protocol, guideline, or definition links for the whole CarePlan. R6 removes both without a same-level replacement in the CarePlan definition. This is an old-valid/new-invalid break and a traceability risk, not just cleanup of an obscure child path. The preferred R6 home may be a referenced request, RequestOrchestration, PlanDefinition, Provenance, or extension, but that is not evident from the base CarePlan StructureDefinition. Keeping the optional fields as deprecated while documenting the new pattern would be a modest less-breaking base design.
keyEvidence: R4 CarePlan.instantiatesCanonical is 0..* canonical targeting PlanDefinition, Questionnaire, Measure, ActivityDefinition, or OperationDefinition.
R4 CarePlan.instantiatesUri is 0..* uri for external protocols or definitions.
R6 CarePlan has no instantiatesCanonical or instantiatesUri element.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral, but protocol and definition traceability can affect CDS, audit, quality, and explanation. The absence of a visible base replacement keeps the removal concerning.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: R4 instances with root instantiatesCanonical or instantiatesUri fail strict R6 validation and can lose protocol linkage unless another representation is chosen.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Yes. R6 could retain both optional fields as deprecated and point to the preferred R6 representation. The tradeoff is continued legacy workflow surface area and possibly multiple places to find protocol links, but the fields are optional and do not create direct conflict with a replacement CarePlan element.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing High impact and Partial alternative judgment; the fresh review treats the missing replacement and modest deprecated-field alternative as strong enough for Revisit.

findings.title: CarePlan.status required value set adds ended

oldState.summary: Required binding to request-status|4.0.1 with draft, active, on-hold, revoked, completed, entered-in-error, and unknown.

flags.isModifierReason: Status includes entered-in-error, meaning the resource should not be treated as valid.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 CarePlan.status used the common request-status set without `ended`.

newState.summary: Required binding to request-status|6.0.0-ballot4, adding ended.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: Comparison used package CodeSystem concepts and ValueSet compose, not a terminology server expansion.

flags.isModifierReason: Status includes entered-in-error, meaning the resource should not be treated as valid.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 permits `status="ended"`, defined as no longer to be acted upon without distinguishing degree of action already undertaken.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is not an R4→R6 validation break because all R4 status codes remain present. It is a required-binding widening that creates R6→R4 representability risk and runtime risk for enum-based code compiled against the R4 set.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Status controls whether a care plan is actionable; mapping `ended` incorrectly to completed or revoked can change operational behavior.

justification.inferredGoal: Represent an ended request without forcing systems to choose completed or revoked.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: adding `ended` widens the R6 required value set and does not make any R4 status code invalid.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The change is additive from the R4-to-R6 validation perspective: all R4 CarePlan.status codes remain valid in R6. The new `ended` code fills a meaningful lifecycle gap, while the reported risks are reverse-conversion and runtime-enum risks rather than old-valid/new-invalid base-design breakage. Treating extension or conversion guidance as a backward-compatible alternative would misclassify the issue.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Because this finding is not an R4-to-R6 breaking base-design issue, there is no applicable less-breaking base alternative to rate. R6-to-R4 systems still need a policy for preserving or mapping `ended`, but that is a mitigation for reverse compatibility, not a reason to mark a base R6 alternative as available.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: No less-breaking R4-to-R6 base design is needed; R6-to-R4 conversion and enum handling still need explicit policy for `ended`.

evidence.detail: R4 required binding is request-status|4.0.1.
R6 required binding is request-status|6.0.0-ballot4.
R6 request-status adds ended: no longer to be acted upon and does not differentiate degree of action already undertaken.

examples.examplesMd: The R6 example is valid against the R6 required value set but the status code is outside the R4 CarePlan.status required value set.

findings.narrativeMd: The status binding is widened, not narrowed. Existing R4 statuses still validate in R6, but R6 introduces a new lifecycle value that R4 systems do not know. This mainly affects reverse conversion, enum generation, database constraints, dashboards, and switch statements that assumed the R4 status set was closed.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4→R6: no old-valid/new-invalid status code was found. R6→R4: `status="ended"` is not representable as a valid R4 CarePlan.status code without a mapping choice such as revoked, completed, or an extension, each of which changes meaning.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R4→R6, update generated enums and tests to include `ended`. For R6→R4, define a policy and preferably preserve the original `ended` value in an extension if mapping to a nearest R4 status. Test downstream workflow rules that decide whether a plan is actionable.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Adding `ended` is clinically/operationally useful, but it could have been modeled as a profile or extension for compatibility. The tradeoff is that base interoperability around ended plans would remain weak.

freshReview.narrativeMd: The required status binding is widened by adding `ended`; the R4 status codes remain available in the R6 request-status system, so this is not an R4-to-R6 validation break for existing CarePlans. It still matters because `status` is required and a modifier: closed enums, switch statements, workflow state machines, and R6-to-R4 gateways must handle `ended` deliberately. The added lifecycle state is reasonable and the base model preserved old codes, so this is migration work rather than a standards-design problem.
keyEvidence: R4 CarePlan.status is 1..1 code with required binding to request-status|4.0.1.
R6 CarePlan.status is 1..1 code with required binding to request-status|6.0.0-ballot4.
R6 request-status adds ended, defined as no longer to be acted upon without differentiating degree of action already undertaken.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral. Because the change is additive for R4 content, maturity does not create a revisit concern, though the modifier status path makes runtime handling important.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: runtime/API/codegen: R6 consumers with closed R4-era status enums or workflow logic must handle ended; R6-to-R4 loss applies when no exact R4 status exists.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Not applicable for R4-to-R6 base compatibility. R6 kept the R4 codes and only added a new one. Profiles, extensions, or ConceptMaps can help down-conversion, but they are mitigations rather than less-breaking base R6 designs.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing Medium impact and Not applicable alternative judgment; the fresh review emphasizes that the additive modifier-code change is real but proportionate.

findings.title: CarePlan.intent required value set adds directive

oldState.summary: Required binding to care-plan-intent|4.0.1 with proposal, plan, order, and option.

flags.isModifierReason: Intent changes the interpretation of descriptive attributes.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 CarePlan.intent excluded `directive` even though the broader request-intent code system already contained it.

newState.summary: Required binding to care-plan-intent|6.0.0-ballot4 adding directive.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: Comparison used ValueSet compose content; no terminology server expansion was needed for the explicit include list.

flags.isModifierReason: Intent changes the interpretation of descriptive attributes.

semanticText.comment: Intent is expected to be immutable; changing proposal to plan/order should create a new basedOn instance.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 CarePlan.intent allows `directive`, and adds comment text emphasizing immutability of intent transitions.

facts.oldValue: No immutability guidance in the CarePlan.intent comment.
facts.newValue: Intent is expected to be immutable; new instances should be created when intent changes.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 CarePlan instances remain valid with respect to intent codes, but an R6 CarePlan with `intent="directive"` is outside the R4 required value set. Runtime code compiled against the R4 CarePlanIntent enum may reject or mishandle the new code.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: `directive` can reflect legally or clinically binding patient/related-person instructions, so lossy mapping to plan/order/proposal can be unsafe.

justification.inferredGoal: Permit CarePlan to represent directive-level intent consistently with the request-intent code system.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: adding `directive` widens the R6 required value set and preserves all R4 CarePlan.intent codes.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Base support for `directive` is reasonable because it represents a distinct level of authority and the R4 codes remain valid in R6. The compatibility problem is that R6 directive instances cannot be represented directly in R4 and may surprise enum-based consumers, not that existing R4 instances become invalid. Under the calibration rules, that makes backward-compatible alternative availability not applicable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: No R4-to-R6 base-design alternative is applicable because this is a target-version expressiveness increase rather than a breaking change to R4-valid content. Extensions, ConceptMaps, or conversion policies may help R6-to-R4 workflows, but they are mitigations rather than less-breaking base R6 designs for this finding.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: No less-breaking R4-to-R6 base design is needed; reverse conversion must avoid silently coercing directive intent.

evidence.detail: R4 CarePlan.intent required binding includes proposal, plan, order, and option.
R6 CarePlan.intent required binding includes proposal, plan, order, option, and directive.
R6 care-plan-intent explicitly includes directive.
R6 request-intent defines directive as an instruction authored by a Patient or RelatedPerson.

examples.examplesMd: The example is R6-valid by binding but not R4-valid because R4 CarePlan.intent excludes directive.

findings.narrativeMd: The required CarePlan.intent set is widened by adding `directive`. That is not a forward validation break for R4 data, but it is material for reverse conversion and for generated enums. Because intent is a modifier element, systems must not treat a directive as if it were merely a plan or proposal.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4→R6: existing R4 intent codes remain valid. R6→R4: `directive` has no valid R4 CarePlan.intent representation. Runtime risk comes from required binding enforcement, exhaustive switch statements, and business rules that use intent to decide authority.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Update R6 enum handling and UI/business logic to recognize directive. For R6→R4, do not silently coerce directive to plan/order/proposal; preserve the original value using an extension or require human/policy review.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The new code is likely justified for expressiveness, but base-level inclusion is not backward-compatible for R4 consumers. A profile or extension could have staged the change, at the cost of less consistent support.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R6 adds `directive` to the required CarePlan.intent binding while retaining the R4 intent codes. That does not invalidate R4 instances, but `intent` is required and a modifier, and directive-level authority is not safely interchangeable with proposal, plan, order, or option. Implementers need enum, UI, authorization, and R6-to-R4 policy updates. Adding the code in the base value set is a reasonable way to support directive CarePlans, so the break is mainly reverse-conversion and runtime readiness rather than a reason to revisit the R6 design.
keyEvidence: R4 CarePlan.intent required binding includes proposal, plan, order, and option.
R6 CarePlan.intent required binding includes proposal, plan, order, option, and directive.
R6 request-intent defines directive as an instruction authored by a Patient or RelatedPerson.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral. The safety/legal meaning of directive keeps the runtime and reverse-conversion concern meaningful, but the additive nature keeps the base design proportionate.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: runtime/API/codegen: closed intent enums and business rules must recognize directive; R6-to-R4 loss applies because R4 CarePlan.intent has no exact directive code.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Not applicable for R4-to-R6 base compatibility. R6 retained all R4 intent codes. Using an extension or profile for directive would ease reverse compatibility but would weaken consistent base support for a distinct authority level.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing Medium impact and Not applicable alternative judgment; the fresh review agrees on the reverse/runtime risk but not on any need for a less-breaking base alternative.

findings.title: CarePlan.basedOn can now reference ServiceRequest, RequestOrchestration, and NutritionOrder

oldState.narrativeMd: In R4, `basedOn` linked a CarePlan to another CarePlan it fulfilled.

newState.summary: 0..* Reference to CarePlan, ServiceRequest, RequestOrchestration, or NutritionOrder.

semanticText.definition: A higher-level request resource (i.e. a plan, proposal or order) that is fulfilled in whole or in part by this care plan.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 generalizes `basedOn` to higher-level request resources beyond CarePlan.

facts.oldValue: A care plan that is fulfilled in whole or in part by this care plan.
facts.newValue: A higher-level request resource (i.e. a plan, proposal or order) that is fulfilled in whole or in part by this care plan.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This target expansion does not invalidate R4 CarePlan references in R6. It does create R6→R4 risk because R4 basedOn cannot validly point to ServiceRequest, RequestOrchestration, or NutritionOrder. Runtime risk exists for code that assumed every basedOn target was another CarePlan.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Incorrect handling of basedOn can break fulfillment chains and provenance of care plans from orders or proposals.

justification.inferredGoal: Represent CarePlans fulfilling higher-level requests, proposals, or orders.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: the R6 target list is widened and existing R4 CarePlan basedOn references remain valid.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Expanding `basedOn` to higher-level request resources is aligned with the R6 definition and does not invalidate R4 instances that reference another CarePlan. The reported risk is for R6-to-R4 representability and for runtime assumptions that every target is a CarePlan. Since this is additive for R4-to-R6 base compatibility, the backward-compatible alternative question is not applicable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: There is no applicable less-breaking base design to preserve R4 instances because the old target remains allowed. R6-to-R4 conversions may need extensions or policy for ServiceRequest, RequestOrchestration, and NutritionOrder targets, but those are reverse-conversion mitigations rather than base R6 alternatives.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: No less-breaking R4-to-R6 base alternative is needed; non-CarePlan R6 targets create only reverse-conversion and target-dispatch costs.

evidence.detail: R4 basedOn targetProfile is CarePlan only.
R6 basedOn adds ServiceRequest, RequestOrchestration, and NutritionOrder.

examples.examplesMd: The R6 example uses an allowed R6 target that violates the R4 target profile for CarePlan.basedOn.

findings.narrativeMd: `basedOn` is widened from CarePlan-only to a broader workflow reference. This is not a forward validation break, but it is important for cross-version conversion and for code that dereferences `basedOn` assuming a CarePlan resource. It also changes the semantic scope from plan-to-plan fulfillment to fulfillment of orders/proposals.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4→R6: existing CarePlan references remain valid. R6→R4: non-CarePlan basedOn references are not valid against the R4 StructureDefinition. Codegen may still use a Reference type, but generated target-union metadata, validation, and business dispatch logic must handle the new targets.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Update R6 validators, search logic, and dereference code to accept the new target profiles. For R6→R4, either preserve non-CarePlan targets in an extension, create intermediary CarePlan resources only when clinically justified, or flag records for manual conversion.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Because this is additive for R4→R6, it is relatively compatible. The main missing compatibility aid is a standard reverse-conversion policy for non-CarePlan targets.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `basedOn` is widened from CarePlan-only to CarePlan, ServiceRequest, RequestOrchestration, or NutritionOrder. Existing R4 basedOn references to CarePlan remain valid in R6, and the element shape and cardinality are unchanged. Code that consumes new R6 data must not assume every target is another CarePlan, and down-conversion of non-CarePlan targets needs policy, but that is the normal cost of additive expressivity rather than an R4-to-R6 compatibility problem.
keyEvidence: R4 CarePlan.basedOn is 0..* Reference(CarePlan).
R6 CarePlan.basedOn is 0..* Reference(CarePlan, ServiceRequest, RequestOrchestration, NutritionOrder).
The R6 definition generalizes basedOn to a higher-level request resource fulfilled by the CarePlan.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral. Since no R4 target was removed, maturity does not add stability concern for this path.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss: only R6 instances using ServiceRequest, RequestOrchestration, or NutritionOrder targets lack a base R4 representation; old R4 CarePlan targets remain valid.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Not applicable. A less-breaking R6 base design is not needed because the old target remains allowed. Rejecting the added targets would reduce R6 workflow expressivity and would only help reverse conversion.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing report's reverse/runtime risk, but disagree with treating this as a material R4-to-R6 problem; the fresh review judges the additive target widening as No problem.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: R6 CarePlan is present with the same canonical URL, id, kind, type, abstract flag, baseDefinition, and derivation. Status changed from draft to active but does not create an identity break.
For surviving local CarePlan-specific elements, no min/max cardinality tightening or relaxation was found. Element removals/additions/replacements are reported separately as findings.

No surviving local CarePlan element changed `isModifier`. The removed R4 inline `activity.detail.doNotPerform` modifier child is covered by the activity.detail removal finding; inherited base modifier changes are out of scope.

No material local summary-flag change was found among surviving CarePlan-specific elements. The visible `modifierExtension` summary flag change is inherited from base DomainResource/Extension handling and excluded.

No surviving local CarePlan invariant was strengthened. R4 `cpl-3` disappeared because the `detail`/`reference` alternative was removed/replaced, which is covered in activity findings. Base `dom-*`, `ele-1`, and extension constraint changes are inherited and out of scope.
No CarePlan-local fixed value, pattern value, or default value change was identified.
No CarePlan-local maxLength, regex, minValue, or maxValue change was identified.
No CarePlan-local slicing changes were identified.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: UI labels and documentation that excluded devices as contributors should be updated, but no instance transform is required.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Description comment clarifies that CarePlan.description is not the whole plan narrative
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The element type and cardinality remain unchanged. The new comment is guidance, not a computable constraint.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Systems that used `description` as the sole human-readable plan should review whether `text` should carry the full narrative, but strict validation is unaffected.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The canonical identity, kind, type, baseDefinition, derivation, and abstract flag are stable. Status maturity affects governance expectations but not instance wire format by itself.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Consumers may treat the R6 resource as more mature, but this is not a structural break.
